name: Bosnian Pyramids
hook: Natural Miocene hills at Visoko, promoted as pyramids first ~12,000 and later ~34,000 years old.
claim: In October 2005, businessman Semir Osmanagić announced Visočica and neighbouring hills near Visoko as step pyramids built about 12,000 years ago by an early European civilization; he later added an underground 'Ravne tunnel' network.

claimed_age.label: ~12,000 yr (2005) to ~33,800 BP (2025 preprint)
claimed_age.basis: ~12,000 yr at the Oct 2005 announcement; ~34,000 yr claimed by 2015; a 2025 foundation preprint calibrates one radiocarbon sample (Kyiv IHME-3734, 29,200±400 BP) to ~33,800 cal BP, not independently replicated.

accepted_age.label: Natural landform: Late Miocene lacustrine/fluvial sediment
accepted_age.basis: Identified on site as Late Miocene lacustrine/fluvial deposits (Schoch 2006), consistent with the Sarajevo-Zenica Basin's Miocene freshwater facies (Sant et al. 2018); S7 does not name Visoko.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: No monumental construction or complex society is documented in the Balkans during the Late Pleistocene; the record is of small, mobile hunter-gatherer groups.

key_proponents: Bosnian Pyramid of the Sun Foundation

unambiguous_signal.note: Natural sedimentary hills (a landform geologists call 'flatirons'); 2006 Tuzla cores and Schoch's visit describe the 'blocks' as conglomerate/clay/sandstone, not the poured concrete Osmanagić claims.

documented_context.note: Excavation was run by the foundation without standard stratigraphic recording; Schoch (2006) reports undocumented fossils being destroyed as crews shaped the hills.

multiple_dating_methods.note: No numeric dating of the formations had been published by outside scientists within five years of the 2005 claim; Schoch's 2006 account is sedimentological/paleontological observation, not dating.

multiple_labs.note: No dates existed within 5 yr of the claim. A 2025 program sent samples to six outside AMS/U-Th labs; the foundation alone chose samples/contexts, and no outside team has resampled independently.

professional_recovery.note: Osmanagić, a businessman with no archaeology/geology credentials, led the dig; permits existed from the start, but a 2026 paper calls 2025's Ravne 6 dig its first 'formally authorized' excavation.

peer_reviewed_report.note: The original claim appeared in a self-published Sarajevo book (Bosanska Piramida Sunca, 2005), not a peer-reviewed venue.

material_accessible.note: Osmanagić invited outside specialists (e.g. Schoch) to visit and the site is a public park, but excavation control and sample custody stayed with the foundation.

independent_teams.note: In 2006, no independent research group had corroborated artificial construction; the European Association of Archaeologists and Bosnian heritage professionals opposed the project instead.

proponent_stake.note: Osmanagić's foundation solicits public and state-company donations and profits from tourism and souvenirs built on the pyramid claim; he had already authored a book on Maya pyramids.

objections.text: The 'pyramid' hills are natural Late Miocene lacustrine and fluvial sediments of the Sarajevo-Zenica Basin, not human-built structures.
objections.outcome_note: Confirmed by on-site inspection and consistent with independent regional basin stratigraphy (Sant et al. 2018); S7 does not discuss Visoko specifically.

objections.text: Excavation was directed by a businessman's private foundation, not an accredited team; the European Association of Archaeologists called it 'a cruel hoax on an unsuspecting public' with no place in genuine science.
objections.outcome_note: No accredited academic institution has endorsed the excavation; the foundation still runs it two decades on.

objections.text: Fossiliferous Late Miocene strata (undocumented plant and animal remains) are being damaged or destroyed as crews carve the hills into stepped pyramid form, with no paleontological recording.
objections.outcome_note: Firsthand account by an invited geologist visiting during active excavation; no published rebuttal or counter-survey was found.

objections.text: Osmanagić says the conglomerate 'blocks' are poured concrete; University of Tuzla geologists analyzing his own 2006 core samples instead found ordinary conglomerate, clay and sandstone layers matching nearby mountains.
objections.raised_by: University of Tuzla geologists; R. M. Schoch
objections.outcome_note: Materials scientist Joseph Davidovits endorsed the poured-concrete idea, but no independent petrographic study supports it; Osmanagić's 2025 paper still describes the material as breccia, clay binder and sandstone.

objections.text: The foundation selected and described the context for every sample behind its ~33,800 BP claim; although six outside AMS/U-Th labs measured them, no independent team has sampled or interpreted the site's dating context.
objections.outcome_note: Radiocarbon and U-Th measurements came from accredited outside labs (e.g. Kyiv, Beta Analytic, Kiel), but sample choice, context and interpretation stayed with the foundation; not yet in a mainstream geology journal.

objections.text: Wood from Ravne 6 fill, AMS-dated by the foundation's 2025 dig, clusters in the late 15th-16th century CE; excavators cite possible secondary deposition, old wood, or reuse, and date the wood, not the tunnel's cutting.
objections.outcome_note: The authors themselves limit the result to activity within the excavated section and list contamination-type caveats; it neither confirms nor rules out an older origin for the wider tunnel network.

objections.text: Finite ages of 24,800-34,000 BP match what slight younger contamination would give in radiocarbon-dead samples; two dates on the same tunnel wood differ by 3,000+ years (34,000±1,500 vs 30,600±525 BP).
objections.outcome_note: No published study has tested the dated organics for contamination or shown they relate to a specific construction event; the age-contamination relationship is well established (Stuiver & Polach 1977).

status_note: Geologists identify the hills as natural Miocene sediment; no part of the claim has passed mainstream peer review. The foundation's 2025-26 dating program is unreplicated, and no independent team has studied the Ravne tunnels.
what_settled_it: In early 2006, University of Tuzla geologists analyzing Osmanagić's own cores found ordinary conglomerate/clay/sandstone matching nearby mountains; Schoch's visit found natural Late Miocene deposits. The EAA rejected the project later in 2006; no peer-reviewed report has overturned this.

timeline.event: Osmanagić publishes 'Bosanska Piramida Sunca', announcing Visočica and neighbouring hills as ~12,000-year-old step pyramids.
Osmanagić secures digging permits, drills core samples, and founds the Bosnian Pyramid of the Sun Foundation.
University of Tuzla geologists analyze Osmanagić's own core samples, finding ordinary conglomerate/clay/sandstone layers matching nearby mountains.
Geologist Robert Schoch visits at Osmanagić's invitation and identifies the hills as natural Late Miocene sediments.
Science publishes Bohannon's 'Mad About Pyramids' news feature on the controversy.
European Association of Archaeologists issues an open letter calling the project a hoax; Science reports it.
Osmanagić tells the press fossilized leaves were dated to ~34,000 years, extending his original ~12,000-year claim.
Independent stratigraphic study documents the Sarajevo-Zenica Basin's Miocene freshwater sediments, consistent with the 'pyramid' hills' geology.
Academic study in Nova Religio analyzes Visoko as a commodified New Age pilgrimage site built on the pyramid and tunnel claims.
Osmanagić's foundation publishes a revised age claim (~33,800 BP from a calibrated radiocarbon date) and describes the 'blocks' as breccia, clay and sandstone.
The foundation's own AMS-dated Ravne 6 tunnel wood clusters in the late 15th-16th century CE; the authors limit the result to the sampled wood.

falsifier: Independent, peer-reviewed petrographic or geochemical analysis by geologists with no foundation ties, replicated at a second lab, showing the 'blocks' have an artificial fabric or cementation inconsistent with the surrounding Miocene bedrock.

confidence_note: Schoch, the EAA response, Woodard and both EarthArXiv preprints were read in full. The 2005 Osmanagić books, Nova Religio full text and S7's abstract remain unread, known only via citation/metadata.
corrections: The brief's 'flatirons' term is accurate — geologist Paul Heinrich uses it for this landform. What it omits: Osmanagić's own crews actively carved and terraced the hillsides to sharpen the stepped-pyramid look (Schoch 2006).

The claimed age changed over time: ~12,000 yr at the 2005 announcement, ~34,000 yr by 2015 (per Osmanagić), refined to ~33,800 cal BP for one sample in a 2025 preprint — not one fixed figure throughout.
Science's coverage was not one 2006 article: Bohannon wrote two News pieces (Sept. and Dec. 2006), and Science also published a letter from geologist Robert Schoch describing his own site visit.
notes: EAA's 2006 quote (via S2): the project is 'a cruel hoax on an unsuspecting public [which] has no place in the world of genuine science.' independent_methods_count (5): landform shape/orientation; the poured-concrete/clay-binder block claim (endorsed by materials scientist Joseph Davidovits); tunnel features; the foundation's radiocarbon program; its U-series/soil-pedogenesis program. S8 was also published in a non-geology journal outside normal peer review. No part of the claim has appeared in a mainstream geology or archaeology journal as of 2026. Plates omitted: no matching Commons image found.
